newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian reformers poised for landslide poll win.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian reformers poised for landslide poll win.

text.p: Opinion polls on Friday showed Bulgaria's anti-communist UDF cruising towards overwhelming victory on the eve of early elections forced by a wave of unrest it led three months ago.

Two polls gave the Union of Democratic Forces around half of public support, enough to secure an absolute majority in a new parliament and a mandate to press ahead with market reforms demanded by international lenders as a condition of aid to rescue the devastated economy.

Gallup International gave the UDF 54 percent, compared with 24 for the ex-communist Socialist Party, which handed power to an interim government after a midwinter explosion of discontent at rocketing inflation and mass poverty.
Bulgarian pollsters Sova-5 gave the UDF 47 percent and the Socialists 19, still more than enough to give the UDF most deputies in the 240-seat parliament.

The Socialists, who won 1994 elections, stand accused of economic mismanagement that has fuelled inflation of more than 2,000 percent a year. But they still command loyalty among many old people who lived most of their lives under communist dictatorship until 1989.
Support for the UDF, in contrast, is concentrated among the under-40s, said Sova-5.

A UDF victory is expected to herald a crash programme of economic reform, years after most other east European countries took the same route. Privatisations and closures of loss-making state firms will cause even more hardship among impoverished Bulgarians, at least at first.

Also on the agenda might be a referendum on restoring the country's long-exiled monarchy, an idea bitterly opposed by the Socialists. King Simeon visited the country this week and lent his voice to reform.
Monarchists are represented in one of three small coalitions hoping to attract more than the four percent of votes required to win a place in parliament.
The National Salvation Union, which also represents the country's ethnic Turkish minority, scored 6.5 percent and five percent in the Gallup and Sova-5 polls respectively.
The Euro-Left, a new grouping including some defectors from the Socialists, registered 6.5 and seven and the Bulgarian Business Block about four and five percent.

Its outcome a foregone conclusion, the election has failed to ignite the passions of a demoralised public who in January and February besieged the Socialist-dominated parliament and took to the streets to demand polls two years ahead of schedule.
Some 72 percent said they had not bothered to read the rival parties' election campaign programmes, according to Sova-5.
